models.name: AASIST
models.summary: Looks at the raw audio waveform and uses a graph network to link patterns across time and frequency that speech synthesis leaves behind.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, SincNet-style filters and residual encoder, spectral and temporal graph attention with a max graph operation, two-way classifier
models.description: AASIST (Jung et al., ICASSP 2022) listens to the raw waveform and builds graphs over the frequency bands and over the time steps, then uses graph attention to weigh which parts of the signal look artificial. Speech made by synthesis often leaves small traces in the spectrum or in the timing, and the authors designed one network that catches both without needing an ensemble. The released weights were trained only on the ASVspoof 2019 LA training split. It is a compact standard baseline: scored on the full ASVspoof 2019 LA eval set here it reaches an equal error rate (EER) of 1.58%, against 0.83% in the paper, but on In-the-Wild, which it never saw, it sits close to chance (EER 44.0%).
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: AASIST: Audio Anti-Spoofing Using Integrated Spectro-Temporal Graph Attention Networks

models.name: AASIST3
models.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (repo LICENSE; the model card says CC BY-NC 4.0)
models.summary: An AASIST upgrade that feeds in features from a pretrained speech model and uses a newer layer type (KAN); the released weights are a weak baseline.
models.architecture: Pre-emphasised 16 kHz window, wav2vec 2.0 XLSR-53 features, KAN bridge and residual encoder, spectral and temporal graph attention, four inference branches, KAN output layer, two-way classifier
models.description: AASIST3 (Borodin et al., 2024) was built for the ASVspoof 2024 challenge. It extends AASIST by feeding in features from a pretrained speech model (wav2vec 2.0 XLSR-53) and by swapping some ordinary layers for Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) layers, a newer kind of learned layer. The released weights saw ASVspoof 2019 LA, ASVspoof 5, MLAAD and M-AILABS after the front end was pretrained on Common Voice, BABEL and Multilingual LibriSpeech, so the benchmark refuses it on any MLAAD-based evalset. The repository says these weights are not the ones behind the paper's numbers, and the Speech DF Arena measures them at 28 to 32% EER on In-the-Wild and ASVspoof 2021, so it is kept here as a weak multilingual baseline, not a strong one.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: AASIST3: KAN-Enhanced AASIST Speech Deepfake Detection using SSL Features and Additional Regularization for the ASVspoof 2024 Challenge

models.name: AASIST-L
models.summary: A much smaller version of AASIST that works on the raw waveform with the same graph idea but far fewer parameters, so it runs cheaply.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, SincNet-style filters and residual encoder, spectral and temporal graph attention with a max graph operation, two-way classifier (lightweight configuration)
models.description: AASIST-L is the lightweight variant of AASIST from the same paper (Jung et al., ICASSP 2022). It uses the same graph idea on the raw waveform with far fewer parameters, which the authors put at about 85 thousand, so it is cheap to run. Its released weights were trained only on the ASVspoof 2019 LA training split. Scored on the full ASVspoof 2019 LA eval set here it reaches an EER of 1.49% (paper 0.99%), and on In-the-Wild it is near chance (EER 44.9%), so it shows how little a small model trained on one corpus carries over to other data.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: AASIST: Audio Anti-Spoofing Using Integrated Spectro-Temporal Graph Attention Networks

models.name: AltFreezing
models.summary: Watches a face video in 3D and alternately freezes its space and time filters during training, so it learns both visual glitches and unnatural motion.
models.architecture: Face video clip, 3D convolutional network whose spatial and temporal weight groups are frozen alternately during training, two-way classifier
models.description: AltFreezing (Wang et al., CVPR 2023) looks at short face video clips with a 3D convolutional network, so it can pick up both visual flaws in single frames and unnatural motion between frames. Such a network tends to lean on one kind of clue, so during training the authors alternately freeze its space-related weights and its time-related weights, which forces it to learn both. The released weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (compression level not stated). It is built for generalising to unseen manipulations, but it is blocked in this benchmark: the weights are only on RecDrive and Baidu, upstream issues report the file gone, and there is no adapter yet.

paper.title: AltFreezing for More General Video Face Forgery Detection

models.name: AntiDeepfake MMS-300M
models.summary: A multilingual speech model (MMS-300M) further trained on 74k hours of real and fake audio in over 100 languages to tell them apart.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows (zero mean, unit variance), MMS-300M wav2vec 2.0 front end, mean pooling over frames, linear layer, two-way classifier
models.description: AntiDeepfake MMS-300M comes from the NII Yamagishi Lab (Ge et al., 2025, "Post-training for Deepfake Speech Detection"). The authors take a speech model that was pretrained on ordinary speech and give it a middle "post-training" stage on a large mix of real and fake speech, so the model learns about artefacts before any task-specific tuning. This one starts from MMS-300M, which was pretrained on about 1,400 languages, and is post-trained on 74 thousand hours from 29 corpora in over 100 languages, including FLEURS, MLAAD, all of ASVspoof 2019 LA, LJSpeech and VoxCeleb2. That wide exposure makes it a strong multilingual candidate for South Asian audio, but the benchmark refuses it on MLAAD-based evalsets and on anything built from FLEURS. The model card reports an In-the-Wild EER of 2.90%.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: Post-training for Deepfake Speech Detection

models.name: AntiDeepfake wav2vec 2.0 small
models.summary: The small English-pretrained wav2vec 2.0 version (95M parameters) of the same post-training recipe, a cheap counterpart to the multilingual model.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows (zero mean, unit variance), wav2vec 2.0 base front end, mean pooling over frames, linear layer, two-way classifier
models.description: AntiDeepfake wav2vec 2.0 small is the smallest model of the NII Yamagishi Lab's AntiDeepfake series (Ge et al., 2025). It is a wav2vec 2.0 base model (95 million parameters) pretrained on English LibriSpeech only, then post-trained on the same 74 thousand hours of real and fake speech from 29 corpora as the MMS-300M model. It decides real versus fake by pooling its speech features over time and passing them to one linear layer. Because the post-training data are identical, comparing it with the MMS-300M version isolates the effect of multilingual pretraining. The model card reports an In-the-Wild EER of 4.24%, against 2.90% for MMS-300M, and the benchmark refuses it on MLAAD-based evalsets and on anything built from FLEURS.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: Post-training for Deepfake Speech Detection

models.name: CORE
models.summary: An Xception image network trained so its internal view of a face stays the same under crops, colour changes and other tweaks.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, Xception CNN trained with a consistency loss across augmented views, two-way classifier
models.description: CORE (Ni et al., CVPRW 2022) is an Xception image network, run here from DeepfakeBench's release, that checks individual face frames. During training it sees the same face under different augmentations, such as crops and colour changes, and a loss term pushes its internal representations of those views to stay close, which the authors say makes them more consistent and relieves overfitting. At test time it is used like a plain Xception classifier, scoring each frame. The released weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23 compression per the DeepfakeBench README), after ImageNet pretraining. It adds one training idea on top of the Xception baseline, so it helps show whether such tricks carry over to South Asian faces.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: CORE: Consistent Representation Learning for Face Forgery Detection

models.name: DF Arena 1B
models.licence: non-commercial (custom LICENSE.txt in the model repo)
models.summary: A large audio model (XLS-R 1B) that pools features from every layer and classifies them with a conformer head; top open model on the Speech DF Arena.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, XLS-R 1B front end, attention pooling over every hidden layer, conformer head, spoof or bona fide classifier
models.description: DF Arena 1B is a universal speech anti-spoofing model released by the Speech DF Arena project (Speech-Arena-2025, 2025), the team behind a public leaderboard for audio deepfake detectors. It runs the audio through the large XLS-R 1B speech model, pools the features of every layer with learned attention weights, and passes them to a conformer, a transformer-style block with convolutions, that makes the call. Its XLS-R front end was pretrained on Common Voice, BABEL, MLS, VoxPopuli and VoxLingua107, and it was then trained on ASVspoof 2019 and 2024, MLAAD, Codecfake, LibriSeVoc, DFADD, CtrSVDD, SpoofCeleb and EnvSDD, so the benchmark refuses it on ASVspoof 2019 LA eval and MLAAD. It is the top open model on that leaderboard, and here it reproduces the model card's In-the-Wild result (EER 0.67% on the full set, against the card's 0.91%).
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: Speech DF Arena: A Leaderboard for Speech DeepFake Detection Models

models.name: DF Arena 500M
models.licence: non-commercial (custom LICENSE.txt in the model repo)
models.summary: The mid-size sibling (XLS-R 300M) of the Speech DF Arena detector, with the same layer pooling and conformer head.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, XLS-R 300M front end, attention pooling over every hidden layer, conformer head, spoof or bona fide classifier
models.description: DF Arena 500M is the mid-size universal speech anti-spoofing model from the Speech DF Arena project (Speech-Arena-2025, 2025). It uses the XLS-R 300M speech model, pools the features of every layer with learned attention weights, and passes them to a conformer head that makes the call. Its front end was pretrained on Common Voice, BABEL, MLS, VoxPopuli and VoxLingua107, and it was then trained on ASVspoof 2019 and 2024, MLAAD, Codecfake, LibriSeVoc, DFADD, CtrSVDD, SpoofCeleb and EnvSDD, so the benchmark refuses it on ASVspoof 2019 LA eval and MLAAD. Here it reproduces the model card's In-the-Wild result (EER 1.51% on the full set, against the card's 1.76%), which makes it a strong, widely trained audio reference.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: Speech DF Arena: A Leaderboard for Speech DeepFake Detection Models

models.name: EfficientNet-B4
models.summary: A standard EfficientNet-B4 image network that looks at cropped face frames and learns visual artefacts of manipulation.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, EfficientNet-B4 CNN, two-way classifier
models.description: EfficientNet-B4 is a standard image network, here DeepfakeBench's single-network version of the detector studied by Bonettini et al. (ICPR 2020), whose paper combines several EfficientNet-B4 variants into an ensemble. It looks at one cropped face frame at a time and learns the visual artefacts of manipulation from examples. The released weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23 compression per the DeepfakeBench README), after ImageNet pretraining. It is a classic image-only baseline for video, and together with Xception it shows how far a plain CNN gets before any special forgery-detection ideas are added.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Video Face Manipulation Detection Through Ensemble of CNNs

models.name: Effort
models.licence: none published (README badge says CC BY-NC 4.0; issue 3 asks for a licence file)
models.summary: Adapts a big pretrained CLIP vision model by tuning only a small part of its weights, keeping its general knowledge while learning to spot fakes.
models.architecture: Aligned 224 px face crop, CLIP ViT-L/14 image encoder with SVD-split weights (principal part frozen, residual part tuned), linear head
models.description: Effort (Yan et al., ICML 2025) adapts a large pretrained CLIP vision model by splitting its weight matrices with singular value decomposition, freezing the main components that hold general knowledge, and training only the small remainder to spot fakes. The authors argue that ordinary fine-tuning overfits to a few fake patterns, and that this split keeps the model's feature space rich enough to generalise. The paper is about AI-generated images in general, and here DeepfakeBench's Effort detector scores face frames. The released weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23) after CLIP pretraining on OpenAI's private data. It is blocked for now because Google Drive refused the weight file as over quota on 2026-10-05, and upstream reports a reproduction gap (Celeb-DF v2 AUC 0.885 against 0.956) and publishes no licence file.
models.input: 224 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Orthogonal Subspace Decomposition for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection

models.name: F3Net
models.summary: Splits each face image into frequency bands (fine versus coarse detail) before an Xception network, since fakes leave traces there that eyes miss.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, DCT frequency-band decomposition (12 input channels), Xception CNN, two-way classifier
models.description: F3Net (Qian et al., ECCV 2020) detects fake faces by looking at frequency, not only at pixels. It splits each face image into bands of fine and coarse detail with a discrete cosine transform and feeds the bands to an Xception network, because manipulation can leave traces in those bands that the eye misses, especially after video compression. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23) after ImageNet pretraining. The detector's yaml names only NeuralTextures, which may not describe the checkpoint, and the benchmark treats it as trained on all of FF++. It is the frequency-cue member of the classic video group.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Thinking in Frequency: Face Forgery Detection by Mining Frequency-aware Clues

models.name: FFD
models.summary: An Xception network with an attention map that highlights which face regions were manipulated and focuses the classifier there.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, Xception CNN with an attention map over manipulated regions, two-way classifier
models.description: FFD (Dang et al., CVPR 2020) is an Xception network with an attention map. The map highlights which parts of the face look manipulated and steers the classifier towards them, and it can also be shown to a person as a rough picture of where the forgery is. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23 per the DeepfakeBench README), after ImageNet pretraining. It is one of the classic image-based detectors in the benchmark, here representing the idea of focusing on the manipulated region, and its scores match the original code closely in the parity check.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: On the Detection of Digital Face Manipulation

models.name: GenD (CLIP ViT-L/14)
models.summary: Fine-tunes a few parameters of a pretrained CLIP vision model on face frames so it still works on deepfakes from unseen datasets.
models.architecture: Aligned face crop at native size, CLIP ViT-L/14 image encoder with only LayerNorm parameters tuned, L2-normalised features, linear head
models.description: GenD (Yermakov et al., WACV 2026) takes a large pretrained CLIP vision model and tunes only its LayerNorm parameters, about 0.03% of the model, so the general knowledge in CLIP stays mostly intact. It also forces the face features onto a sphere with L2 normalisation and metric learning, and each frame gets a real-or-fake probability that is averaged over the video. The released weights were trained on FaceForensics++ only, after CLIP pretraining on OpenAI's private image-text data. The authors report that it beats more complex methods in average cross-dataset AUROC over 14 benchmarks, which makes it the main generalisation-first video model here. Its adapter runs end to end, but parity with upstream is not yet checked.
models.input: native-size aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Deepfake Detection that Generalizes Across Benchmarks

models.name: GenD (Perception Encoder L/14)
models.summary: The same GenD recipe built on Meta's Perception Encoder instead of CLIP, so the two show how much the backbone matters.
models.architecture: Aligned face crop at native size resized to 224, Meta Perception Encoder L/14 with only LayerNorm parameters tuned, L2-normalised features, linear head
models.description: This is GenD's second released backbone: the same recipe as GenD (Yermakov et al., WACV 2026), built on Meta's Perception Encoder instead of CLIP. Only the LayerNorm parameters are tuned, the face features are L2-normalised, and a video's score is the mean over its frames. The released weights were trained on FaceForensics++ only, after Meta's pretraining of the encoder on data that is not public, so overlap with our data cannot be checked. Because it differs from the CLIP version only in backbone, comparing the two shows how much the pretrained foundation model matters. Its adapter has not yet been through the parity check.
models.input: native-size aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Deepfake Detection that Generalizes Across Benchmarks

models.name: HAVIC
models.summary: Checks whether the sound and the moving face in a video belong together, catching fakes where lips, voice or expression do not match.
models.architecture: 16-frame windows of 224 px face frames plus 128-bin audio filterbank, audio and video transformer encoders pretrained on real videos, audio-visual interaction module, MLP classifier, one logit per window
models.description: HAVIC (CVPR 2026 Findings) is an audio-visual detector that asks whether the sound and the moving face in a video belong together. It first learns what coherent audio, video and cross-modal timing look like by pretraining on real videos only, then combines the audio and visual features to score a clip, which should help against fakes whose lips, voice or expression disagree. Its weights were pretrained on LRS2 and fine-tuned on a random 70% of FakeAVCeleb, and because that split's item list is unpublished the benchmark refuses it on FakeAVCeleb. It is the only open audio-visual detector here, and it needs videos of at least 3.2 seconds with a face in 16 sampled frames, so HiDF's 3-second clips are too short.
models.input: native-size face-box crops at 5 frames per second (up to 50), with the audio under them

paper.title: Leave No Stone Unturned: Uncovering Holistic Audio-Visual Intrinsic Coherence for Deepfake Detection

models.name: LipForensics
models.summary: Watches only the mouth region over time and flags lip movements that look unnatural, a cue that holds across many kinds of fakes.
models.architecture: 25-frame clips of 96 px grayscale mouth crops (88 px centre crop), ResNet-18 with 3D stem, multi-scale temporal convolutional network, one logit per clip
models.description: LipForensics (Haliassos et al., CVPR 2021) watches only the mouth. A network is first taught to lipread, so it learns what natural mouth movement looks like, and its temporal part is then fine-tuned to tell real from forged mouth motion. The authors argue this high-level cue holds up across different manipulations and after compression, because it does not depend on low-level artefacts. The released weights were pretrained on LRW and fine-tuned on FaceForensics++ (c23, all four manipulations). It matters here because lip-sync fakes are a focus of this benchmark, though users report that its FF++ numbers do not reproduce, and it needs at least 25 consecutive frames with a detectable face.
models.input: mouth crops from 25 consecutive frames at a time (up to 100 frames per video)

paper.title: Lips Don't Lie: A Generalisable and Robust Approach to Face Forgery Detection

models.name: RECCE
models.summary: Learns to rebuild real faces only, so fake faces rebuild badly; the rebuilding error is what reveals them.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, Xception encoder with a decoder that reconstructs the face and guides attention from the reconstruction, two-way classifier
models.description: RECCE (Cao et al., CVPR 2022) learns what real faces look like by training a decoder to rebuild them from the encoder's features. Fake faces rebuild poorly, and the reconstruction differences are used to guide the classifier, a cue that does not depend on any one manipulation method. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23 per the DeepfakeBench README), after ImageNet pretraining. It is the reconstruction-based detector in the classic video group, and its scores match the original code closely in the parity check.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: End-to-End Reconstruction-Classification Learning for Face Forgery Detection

models.name: SBI
models.licence: research use only (commercial use needs a licence from the authors)
models.summary: Trained on fakes made by blending a real face with a slightly altered copy of itself, which teaches it blending seams instead of one generator's style.
models.architecture: Face box widened by one eighth on each side and resized to 380 px, EfficientNet-B4 CNN, two-way classifier
models.description: SBI (Shiohara and Yamasaki, CVPR 2022) is trained on fakes it makes itself. Each real face is blended with a slightly altered copy of itself, which produces the seams and statistical mismatches that face swaps leave, without using any real deepfake method. The authors argue this makes the network learn general forgery traces instead of the style of one generator. Only the real videos of FaceForensics++ were used, after ImageNet pretraining, and the c23 checkpoint is the one used here. It is a widely cited baseline for generalisation, and its research-only licence means its code is never copied into this repository.
models.input: 380 px face-box crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Detecting Deepfakes with Self-Blended Images

models.name: SPSL
models.summary: Gives an Xception network the phase of the image's frequency spectrum as an extra input, where upsampling in fakes leaves a trace.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, RGB plus phase spectrum of the grey image as a fourth channel, Xception CNN, two-way classifier
models.description: SPSL (Liu et al., CVPR 2021) adds the phase of the image's frequency spectrum as an extra input channel next to the colour image. The authors observe that the upsampling steps in most face forgery methods change that phase in a visible way, so it carries a clue that colour alone hides. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23) after ImageNet pretraining. The detector's yaml lists only FaceSwap, which may not describe the checkpoint, and the benchmark treats it as trained on all of FF++. It is the phase-cue member of the classic video group, and it uses the full Xception network, not the shallower one of the paper.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Spatial-Phase Shallow Learning: Rethinking Face Forgery Detection in Frequency Domain

models.name: SRM
models.summary: Adds a second stream that keeps only fine, high-frequency noise in the image, which manipulation tends to disturb, next to the normal colour stream.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, RGB stream plus a stream of high-frequency noise residuals from SRM filters, Xception CNN with attention linking the two streams, two-way classifier
models.description: SRM (Luo et al., CVPR 2021) argues that ordinary detectors overfit to colour textures that are specific to one forgery method. It therefore adds a second stream that keeps only the fine, high-frequency noise of the image, where tampered and genuine regions tend to differ, and lets the two streams guide each other with attention. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23 per the DeepfakeBench README), after ImageNet pretraining. It is the noise-residual cue in the classic video group, and its scores match the original code closely in the parity check.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: Generalizing Face Forgery Detection with High-frequency Features

models.name: UCF
models.summary: Separates features specific to one forgery method from features common to all forgeries, and scores using only the common ones.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, Xception encoders separating content, method-specific forgery and common forgery features, scored with the common-forgery head only
models.description: UCF (Yan et al., ICCV 2023) tries to generalise to forgery methods it has not seen. It splits what it sees in a face into three parts: features unrelated to forgery, features specific to one manipulation method, and features common to all forgeries. Only the common features are used for the real-or-fake decision, so the score does not depend on the quirks of a particular generator. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on all four FaceForensics++ methods (c23) after ImageNet pretraining. It is the disentangling approach in the classic video group, and its scores match the original code closely in the parity check.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: UCF: Uncovering Common Features for Generalizable Deepfake Detection

models.name: Xception
models.summary: The classic Xception image network applied to cropped face frames, the standard baseline for video deepfake detection.
models.architecture: Aligned 256 px face crop, Xception CNN with depthwise separable convolutions, two-way classifier
models.description: Xception is a standard image network, and this is the face-forgery detector built on it in the FaceForensics++ paper (Rossler et al., ICCV 2019). It looks at one cropped face frame at a time and learns the visual artefacts of manipulation from examples. The released DeepfakeBench weights were trained on FaceForensics++ (c23 per the README, though upstream issue 151 asking whether every checkpoint is c23 is unanswered), after ImageNet pretraining. It is the standard baseline for video deepfake detection and the model the other DeepfakeBench detectors build on. Some users report that DeepfakeBench's released weights do not reproduce its README table.
models.input: 256 px aligned face crops, 32 frames per video

paper.title: FaceForensics++: Learning to Detect Manipulated Facial Images

models.name: XLS-R 300M + AASIST
models.summary: Takes rich features from a big pretrained speech model (XLS-R 300M) and classifies them with an AASIST graph network.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, fine-tuned XLS-R 300M front end, AASIST graph attention back end on the last layer, two-way classifier
models.description: XLS-R + AASIST (Tak et al., Odyssey 2022) puts the AASIST graph network on top of wav2vec 2.0-style speech features, here from the XLS-R 300M model, and fine-tunes the whole thing on spoofing data. The front end was pretrained on real speech only (Common Voice, BABEL, MLS, VoxPopuli and VoxLingua107), and the full network was then trained on the ASVspoof 2019 LA training split alone. The authors report the lowest equal error rates published at the time on ASVspoof 2021 LA and DF. Training on one corpus makes it a clean zero-shot probe on South Asian sets, with no MLAAD or FLEURS in its training. Its adapter replaces the original fairseq code, so parity with upstream is not checked yet.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: Automatic speaker verification spoofing and deepfake detection using wav2vec 2.0 and data augmentation

models.name: XLSR-Mamba
models.summary: Takes XLS-R speech features and reads them forwards and backwards with a Mamba sequence model instead of attention.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, fine-tuned XLS-R 300M front end, dual-column bidirectional Mamba back end (six blocks per direction), two-way classifier
models.description: XLSR-Mamba (Xiao and Das, IEEE SPL 2024) replaces the attention layers of the back end with Mamba, a state space model that reads a sequence efficiently, and runs it forwards and backwards over XLS-R speech features. The front end was pretrained on real speech (Common Voice, BABEL, MLS, VoxPopuli and VoxLingua107), and the released network was trained on the ASVspoof 2019 LA training split alone. The authors report that on In-the-Wild it emerged as the strongest candidate among the systems they compared. Here it runs without the original compiled Mamba kernels, using plain PyTorch stand-ins that are slower, and parity against those kernels is not checked yet.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: XLSR-Mamba: A Dual-Column Bidirectional State Space Model for Spoofing Attack Detection

models.name: XLS-R 300M + SLS
models.licence: none declared (code and weights); a Hugging Face mirror re-hosts the weights as MIT
models.summary: Pools the outputs of all 24 layers of XLS-R with learned attention weights, since different layers hold different spoofing clues.
models.architecture: Raw 16 kHz waveform in 64,600-sample windows, fine-tuned XLS-R 300M front end, learned attention over all 24 layers (SLS), two linear layers, two-way classifier
models.description: XLS-R + SLS (Zhang et al., ACM Multimedia 2024) is built on the observation that different layers of the XLS-R speech model hold different spoofing clues. Its Sensitive Layer Selection (SLS) module pools the outputs of all 24 layers with learned attention weights before a small classifier makes the call. The front end was pretrained on real speech (Common Voice, BABEL, MLS, VoxPopuli and VoxLingua107), and the network was trained on the ASVspoof 2019 LA training split alone. It is the strongest open model trained on that corpus only, so it works as a clean zero-shot probe on every South Asian set. The repository declares no licence, so its code is imported but never copied, and its parity with upstream is not checked yet.
models.input: 4.04 s windows of raw 16 kHz audio

paper.title: Audio Deepfake Detection with Self-Supervised XLS-R and SLS Classifier

datasets.name: ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access
datasets.licence: see LICENSE_text.txt on the DataShare page
datasets.summary: English speech from the VCTK corpus, real clips plus fakes made by text-to-speech and voice conversion systems; the standard audio benchmark.
datasets.scale: 7.6 GB; train, dev and eval with disjoint speakers
generators: 19 attack systems A01 to A19: text-to-speech, voice conversion, and TTS output passed through voice conversion (A13 to A15)
annotations: attack id: A01 to A19 (TTS, VC or TTS+VC)
official split: train, dev, eval (disjoint speakers)
